quail.e: From Middle English quaylen, from Middle Dutch queilen, quēlen, from Old Dutch *quelan, from Proto-West Germanic *kwelan, from Proto-Germanic *kwelaną (“to suffer”).
quail.g: To waste away; to fade, to wither.

quail.e: From Middle English quayle, quaile, quaille, from Anglo-Norman quaille, from Late Latin quaccola (“quail”). (prostitute): So called because the quail was thought to be a very amorous bird.
quail.g: Any of various small game birds of the genera Coturnix, Anurophasis or Perdicula in the Old World family Phasianidae or of the New World fam

quake.e: From Middle English quaken, from Old English cwacian (“to quake, tremble, chatter”), from Proto-Germanic *kwakōną (“to shake, quiver, tremble”), itself likely of imitative origin.

quaking.e: From Middle English quakynge, quakand, from Old English cwaciende (“quaking”), present participle of Old English cwacian (“to quake, tremble”); equivalent to quake + -ing.
quaking.g: Shaking uncontrollably, especially due to fear or awe; trembling or shivering.

qualify.e: Borrowed from Middle French qualifier (“to qualify”). Equivalent to quality + -fy.
qualify.g: To describe or characterize something by listing its qualities.

quality.e: From Middle English qualite, from Old French qualité, from Latin quālitās, quālitātem, from quālis (“of what kind”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷo- (“who, how”). Cicero coined qualitas as a calque to translate the Ancient Greek word ποιότης (poiótēs, “quality”), coined by Plato from ποῖος (poîos, “of what nature, of what kind”).
quality.g: The kind, condition, and/or the set of characteristics of something, as opposed to the quantity of something.

quantity.e: From Middle English quantite, from Old French quantité, from Latin quantitās (“quantity”), from quantus (“how much”).
quantity.g: A fundamental, generic term used when referring to the measurement (count, amount) of a scalar, vector, number of items or to some other way

quarrel.e: From Middle English querele (“altercation, dispute; argument, debate; armed combat; trial by combat; basis for dispute, complaint; claim, legal suit; a lament; illness”), from Anglo-Norman querele and Middle French querele, querelle (“altercation, dispute; basis for dispute; side in a dispute; complaint; accusation; legal suit; lament.
quarrel.g: A dispute or heated argument (especially one that is verbal).

quarrel.e: From Middle English querelen (“to dispute, quarrel; to assert one's claims; to rebel”), from querele (noun); see etymology 1.
quarrel.g: To argue fiercely; to contend; to squabble; to cease to be on friendly terms, to fall out.

quarrelsome.g: Argumentative; fond of or prone to quarreling.

quarry.e: From Middle English quarere, from Medieval Latin quarreria (1266), literally a “place where stones are squared”, from Old French quarrière (compare modern French carrière), from Vulgar Latin *quadraria, from Latin quadrō (“to square”), itself from quadra (“a square”), from quattuor (“four”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres (“four”).
quarry.g: A site for mining stone, such as limestone, or slate.

quarry.e: From Middle English quyrre, querre, quirre, from Anglo-Norman quiree (“entrails of deer placed on the hide and given to dogs of the chase as a reward”) (influenced by cuir (“skin (of an animal)”), from Latin corium (“a hide”)), from coree (“entrails, viscera”), from Vulgar Latin corata (“entrails”), from Latin cor (“heart”).
quarry.g: A part of the entrails of a hunted animal, given to the hounds as a reward.

quart.e: From Middle English quart, quarte, from Old French quarte, carte, from Latin quartus (“one-fourth”).
quart.g: A unit of liquid capacity equal to two pints; one-fourth (quarter) of a gallon. Equivalent to 1.136 liters in the UK and 0.946 liter (liquid

quart.e: From Middle English quarte, querte, from Old Norse kyrt, *kvirt, neuter of Old Norse kyrr, kvirr (“quiet, still, peaceful”), from Proto-Germanic *kwerruz (“calm, satisfied, pacified”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷerh₂- (“heavy”).

quarter.e: From Middle English quarter, from Anglo-Norman quarter, from Latin quartarius, from quartus.

quarter.g: To drive a carriage so as to prevent the wheels from going into the ruts, or so that a rut shall be between the wheels.

quartermaster.e: From Middle English quartermayster, quartermaistre, equivalent to quarter + master. Perhaps reinforced by and merged with Dutch kwartiermeester, kwartier-meester.
quartermaster.g: An officer whose duty is to provide quarters, provisions, storage, clothing, fuel, stationery, and transportation for a regiment or other bo

quartz.e: From German Quarz, from Middle High German (Central East German) quarz, twarc, from a West Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *tvьrdъ ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *twerH- (“to enclose, grab”).
quartz.g: The most abundant mineral on the earth's surface, of chemical composition silicon dioxide, SiO₂. It occurs in a variety of forms, both cryst

quaternion.e: From Middle English quaterniǒun, from Late Latin quaterniō, from quaternī (“four each”) + -iō, from quater (“four times”). The mathematics sense was coined by Irish mathematician and astronomer William Rowan Hamilton in 1843.
quaternion.g: A group or set of four people or things.

queen.e: From Middle English quene, queen, cwen, from Old English cwēn (“queen”), from Proto-West Germanic *kwāni, from Proto-Germanic *kwēniz (“wife, woman”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷénh₂s (“woman”). Generally eclipsed non-native Middle English regina (“queen”), borrowed from Latin rēgīna (“queen”) (see Modern English Regina).
queen.g: The wife, consort, or widow of a king.

quench.e: From Middle English quenchen, from Old English cwenċan, from Proto-Germanic *kwankijaną.
quench.g: To satisfy, especially a literal or figurative thirst.

question.e: From Middle English questioun, from Anglo-Norman questiun, from Old French question, from Latin quaestiōnem, accusative of quaestiō (“a seeking, investigation, inquiry, question”), from quaerere (“to seek, ask, inquire”), of uncertain origin, but possibly from Proto-Italic *kʷaizeō, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷeh₂- (“to acquire”).
question.g: A worded or expressed sentence, phrase, or only a word on its own, which asks for information, a reply, or a response; an interrogative.

question.e: From Middle English questionen, questyonen, partly from Middle French questionner and partly from the noun.
question.g: To ask questions of; to interrogate; to ask for information.

questioning.e: From question + -ing (noun via Middle English questionyng).
questioning.g: The action of asking questions; a survey; an inquiry.

quick.e: From Middle English quik, quic (“living, alive, active”), from Old English cwic (“alive”), from Proto-West Germanic *kwiku (“alive, lively quick”), from Proto-Germanic *kwikwaz (“alive, lively, quick”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʷih₃wós (“alive”), from *gʷeyh₃- (“to live”), *gʷeyh₃w- (“to live”). For semantic development, compare lively.
quick.g: Moving with speed, rapidity or swiftness, or capable of doing so; rapid; fast.

quicken.e: From Middle English quikenen (“to become alive again after dying; to raise (someone) from the dead; to regain consciousness or strength; to give vitality, revive; to regain validity; to nourish; to spare (the life of someone or something); to ignite; to illuminate; of events: to happen more quickly; of clouds: to form”), from quiken (“to come to life.
quicken.g: Senses relating to life or states of activity.

quicken.e: From quick(silver) (“mercury”) + -en (suffix forming verbs from adjectives and nouns).
quicken.g: To apply quicksilver (mercury) to (something); to combine (something) with quicksilver; to quicksilver.

quickly.e: From Middle English quykly, quikliche, quicliche, cwikliche, cwickliche, from Old English cwiculīċe. By surface analysis, quick + -ly.
quickly.g: Rapidly; with speed; fast; with expedition.

quicksand.e: From Middle English quyksande, from Old English cwecesand (“quicksand”), equivalent to quick (“living”) + sand.
quicksand.g: Wet sand that appears firm but in which things readily sink, often found near rivers or coasts.

quiet.e: From Middle English quiete, from Old French quiet (adjective) and quiete (noun), from Latin quiētus, past participle of quiēscere (“to keep quiet, rest”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyeh₁- (“rest”). Largely displaced native English still in the sense of "with little or no sound".
quiet.g: With little or no sound; free of disturbing noise.

quietly.e: From Middle English quietely, quyetly, equivalent to quiet + -ly.

quietness.e: From Middle English quietnes, quietnesse, quietenesse, qwietnesse, qwietenesse, equivalent to quiet + -ness.
quietness.g: Absence of sound; silence or hush.

quit.e: From Middle English quiten, quyten, from Anglo-Norman quitter, Old French quitter, from quitte (“acquitted, quit”), ultimately from Latin quietus, which itself derives from Proto-Indo-European *kʷyéh₁-ti-s, from *kʷyeh₁- (“to rest”).
quit.g: Released from obligation, penalty, etc; free, clear, or rid.
Any of numerous species of small passerine birds native to tropical America.

quite.e: A development of quit, influence by Anglo-Norman quite. For an analogous semantic development from the same root, compare Armenian շատ (šat).
quite.g: To the greatest extent or degree; completely, entirely.
A series of passes made with the cape to distract the bull.

quiver.e: From Middle English quiver, from Anglo-Norman quivre, from Old Dutch cocare (source of Dutch koker, and cognate to Old English cocer (“quiver, case”)), from Proto-West Germanic *kokar (“container”), said to be from Hunnic, possibly from Proto-Mongolic *kökexür (“leather vessel for liquids”); see there for more.
quiver.g: A container for arrows, crossbow bolts or darts, such as those fired from a bow, crossbow or blowgun.

quiver.e: From Middle English quiver, cwiver, from Old English *cwifer, probably related to cwic (“alive”).

quota.e: From Latin quota pars; see Latin quota.
quota.g: A proportional part or share; the share or proportion assigned to each in a division.

quote.e: From Middle English quoten, coten (“to mark (a book) with chapter numbers or marginal references”), from Old French coter, from Medieval Latin quotāre (“to distinguish by numbers, number chapters”), itself from Latin quotus (“which, what number (in sequence)”), from quot (“how many”) and related to quis (“who”).
quote.g: A statement attributed to a person; a quotation.
